topics.title: Communication systems and channels
topics.definition: A communication link moves information from a source to a destination. The transmitter creates a waveform that the channel can carry; the receiver estimates the message from the received waveform.
topics.explanation: A channel may attenuate, distort or add noise. Guided channels confine the wave to cable or fibre. Unguided channels use radio propagation. Digital decisions can regenerate levels, but they cannot guarantee the recovery of a bit already decided incorrectly.
topics.activity: Change attenuation and noise. Compare the clean transmitted waveform with the received one.

topics.title: Uniform sampling
topics.definition: Sampling measures a continuous signal at equally spaced instants. The horizontal spacing is fixed by the clock; sample heights follow the signal.
topics.explanation: Sampling makes time discrete. The amplitudes remain continuous until quantization. For a baseband signal bandlimited to B, choose a rate above 2B and leave room for a practical anti-alias filter.
topics.activity: Start acquisition. Watch each new sample appear at the current measurement time.

topics.title: Aliasing and anti-alias filtering
topics.definition: Different continuous sinusoids can produce exactly the same sample values. This ambiguity is aliasing.
topics.explanation: Lower fs below twice the tone frequency. A slower sinusoid then passes through the same samples. An anti-alias low-pass filter must act before sampling; a later filter cannot undo overlapping spectra.
topics.activity: Lower the sampling rate. Compare the original sinusoid and its sample-equivalent baseband alias.

topics.title: Sinc reconstruction
topics.definition: Ideal reconstruction combines shifted sinc pulses, one for every sample. Each pulse is weighted by that sample value.
topics.explanation: At another sample instant the shifted sinc is zero. Their sum therefore passes through the samples. Exact recovery assumes a properly bandlimited source and an infinite sample sequence; this laboratory uses a finite sum and shows its edge error.
topics.activity: Change the sample rate and compare the source with the finite sinc interpolation.

topics.title: Pulse-amplitude modulation
topics.definition: PAM stores the message in pulse height. In flat-top PAM a held sample keeps the top of each pulse constant.
topics.explanation: Natural PAM multiplies the analog waveform by a gate train, so the pulse top follows the source while the gate is open. Flat-top PAM instead uses the sample value at the opening instant.
topics.activity: Observe the message, clock instants and held pulses on aligned axes.

topics.title: Pulse-width modulation
topics.definition: PWM carries the message in pulse duration. Here every pulse starts at its slot boundary and its trailing edge moves.
topics.explanation: A ramp comparator converts a held voltage into a width. Recover the sample by measuring width and applying the inverse calibration. Keep the width inside its slot to avoid overlap.
topics.activity: Raise the message amplitude and watch pulse widths change while heights remain fixed.

topics.title: Pulse-position modulation
topics.definition: PPM carries the message in a pulse start time relative to a reference clock. Its width and amplitude stay fixed.
topics.explanation: A receiver must know the slot reference, not merely detect a pulse. Timing errors in either the pulse or reference become errors in the recovered message.
topics.activity: Compare pulse positions against the dashed slot references.

topics.title: Hold response and timing jitter
topics.definition: A finite hold spreads each sample into a rectangular pulse. This changes the frequency response as well as the waveform.
topics.explanation: The normalized hold response has sinc droop. A small timing error also changes the sampled voltage by approximately the local slope times that timing error. Steep slopes are more sensitive.
topics.activity: Change hold duration and observe held samples and response attenuation.

topics.title: Uniform quantization and overload
topics.definition: A quantizer replaces every input amplitude by an allowed reconstruction level. The threshold decides which interval contains the sample.
topics.explanation: This model uses midpoint levels over [−1,1) V. In-range error is at most half a step. Beyond the range the end levels saturate, and the half-step bound no longer applies.
topics.activity: Reduce the number of bits, then increase the input beyond full scale. Inspect the staircase and error.

topics.title: PCM encoding and bit rate
topics.definition: PCM samples the waveform, quantizes each sample and assigns a binary word to the level index. The serial channel sends those words as bits.
topics.explanation: The word length is b bits. Each sample adds b bits to the stream, so changing fs and changing b both affect the transmission rate, but only b sets the number of amplitude levels.
topics.activity: Watch a sample become an index, a codeword and serial bits.

topics.title: Companding
topics.definition: A compressor changes amplitude spacing before a uniform quantizer. Small input magnitudes receive finer effective resolution after expansion.
topics.explanation: The µ-law mapping is nonlinear. Without quantization its inverse recovers the input. With quantization, the recovered signal has nonuniform input-referred errors; compression is not lossless quantization.
topics.activity: Change µ and compare the input, compressed waveform and expanded quantized output.

topics.title: Quantization-noise power and SQNR
topics.definition: The uniform-error model treats quantization error as approximately uniform between −Δ/2 and +Δ/2. Its mean square is Δ²/12.
topics.explanation: For a full-scale sinusoid, signal mean square is A²/2. The familiar 6.02b+1.76 dB expression depends on that full-scale sinusoid and the no-overload uniform-error approximation; it is not universal.
topics.activity: Change the bit depth and compare the quantized waveform and measured sample error.

topics.title: Differential PCM
topics.definition: DPCM predicts the current sample and transmits a quantized prediction error. The receiver adds that error to the same prediction.
topics.explanation: The encoder must run a local reconstruction loop. Both predictors use reconstructed samples; otherwise encoder and decoder predictions can drift apart. This model uses the preceding reconstructed sample as its predictor.
topics.activity: Inspect the input and reconstruction while changing the error-quantizer step.

topics.title: Delta modulation
topics.definition: DM sends one bit per sample. One bit raises the estimate by Δ and the other lowers it by Δ.
topics.explanation: A small step produces granular motion near a slowly varying signal. A step that cannot climb fast enough produces slope overload. For a sinusoid, the largest slope is 2πfA.
topics.activity: Reduce Δ until the staircase cannot track the steep part of the sinusoid.

topics.title: Adaptive delta modulation
topics.definition: ADM changes the step according to recent bits. Runs of equal bits suggest a slope that needs a larger step; alternating bits suggest a smaller step.
topics.explanation: This teaching rule doubles the next step after a repeated bit and halves it after a change, with fixed minimum and maximum values. It is an illustrative ADM rule, not a unique standard implementation.
topics.activity: Compare fixed DM with adaptive steps on the same input.

topics.title: Time-division multiplexing
topics.definition: TDM shares a link by assigning different time slots to different sources. The receiver separates slots using the frame clock.
topics.explanation: One frame can carry one sample from each channel plus framing overhead. The number of transmitted bits per frame multiplied by the frame rate gives the total bit rate.
topics.activity: Observe two input signals being interleaved into alternating time slots.

topics.title: Frequency-division multiplexing
topics.definition: FDM assigns each message a different frequency band, so several messages occupy the link at the same time.
topics.explanation: Band-pass filters separate the channels at the receiver. Guard bands allow practical filter transitions. The simple width calculation assumes non-overlapping assigned message bands.
topics.activity: Inspect two frequency-shifted waveforms and their composite signal.

topics.title: ASK and on-off keying
topics.definition: ASK changes carrier amplitude according to the bit. OOK is the special case with carrier present for one symbol and absent for the other.
topics.explanation: An absent carrier is not an absence of a symbol interval. The receiver still needs timing. Average bit energy is half the ON energy when the two bits are equally likely.
topics.activity: Watch the bit stream gate a sinusoidal carrier on and off.

topics.title: Binary phase-shift keying
topics.definition: BPSK uses two opposite carrier phases. A polar mapper turns bits into signs before multiplication by the carrier.
topics.explanation: With phase zero for bit 1 and phase π for bit 0, the signal changes sign at some bit boundaries. Coherent detection needs the carrier phase reference.
topics.activity: Follow each bit and the corresponding phase reversal as new signal is drawn.

topics.title: Binary frequency-shift keying
topics.definition: BFSK selects one sinusoidal frequency for bit 0 and another for bit 1. The carrier amplitude can remain constant.
topics.explanation: Orthogonality concerns the waveform inner product over the symbol interval. For the noncoherent rectangular-tone design here, spacing 1/Tb is sufficient. Other detection and phase conventions can use different spacings.
topics.activity: Watch bit intervals switch between the low and high tones.

topics.title: Bandwidth conventions
topics.definition: A reported bandwidth needs a definition. A raised-cosine passband width is different from the first-null span of rectangular pulses.
topics.explanation: Rectangular pulses have sidelobes beyond the first null. A first-null width is not a strict limit on occupied spectrum. State the pulse shape and bandwidth convention before comparing systems.
topics.activity: Change roll-off and symbol rate; compare the waveform and calculated passband requirement.

topics.title: QPSK and I/Q branches
topics.definition: QPSK maps two bits to one of four signal points. The I branch multiplies cosine; the Q branch multiplies negative sine in the convention used here.
topics.explanation: Gray labels 00,01,11,10 occupy phases 45°,135°,225°,315°. Adjacent symbols differ in one bit. Constellation points represent symbols, not a physical particle orbiting continuously between them.
topics.activity: Watch I, Q and their summed passband signal for consecutive symbols.

topics.title: M-ary PSK
topics.definition: M-PSK packs M phases on a circle. Each symbol carries k=log2M bits when M is a power of two.
topics.explanation: At fixed symbol energy, more phases bring neighbouring points closer. The symbol rate can decrease for a fixed bit rate, but the receiver then needs more energy-to-noise ratio for comparable reliability.
topics.activity: Increase M and compare phase levels, symbol rate and minimum point distance.

topics.title: Square QAM
topics.definition: QAM chooses both in-phase and quadrature amplitudes. For square 16-QAM each axis uses four levels.
topics.explanation: In this model the axis levels are −3a,−a,a,3a and average symbol energy is 10a². Decide a noisy point by the nearest allowed level on each axis under equal-prior AWGN assumptions.
topics.activity: Inspect I/Q level changes and the resulting amplitude and phase variation.

topics.title: Bit rate, symbol rate and spectral efficiency
topics.definition: The bit rate counts bits per second. The symbol rate counts transmitted waveform choices per second. A symbol may represent several bits.
topics.explanation: For uncoded M-ary transmission, Rb=kRs. With full raised-cosine passband width, efficiency is k/(1+α). Coding overhead, guards and implementation details change the usable information efficiency.
topics.activity: Change bits per symbol and roll-off and inspect the rate and bandwidth trade-off.

topics.title: Differential encoding and detection
topics.definition: A differential encoder represents information as changes of encoded state. A differential detector compares consecutive received symbols. These are different operations.
topics.explanation: Use d[k]=b[k] XOR d[k−1] and an agreed reference state. In the phase convention here information 1 reverses the phase. A wrong coherently detected state can corrupt two adjacent differentially decoded bits. Differentially encoded PSK (DEPSK) with coherent decisions and differential decoding is distinct from differential phase detection. For binary DEPSK, Pb = 2p(1−p), where p = Q(√(2Eb/N0)) is the independent coherent-state error probability; ideal differential DBPSK instead has Pb = 0.5 exp(−Eb/N0).
topics.equation: \begin{aligned} d_k&=b_k\oplus d_{k-1},\quad b_k=d_k\oplus d_{k-1}\\ P_b^{\mathrm{DE-BPSK}}&=2p(1-p),\quad p=Q(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0})\\ P_b^{\mathrm{DBPSK}}&=\tfrac12 e^{-E_b/N_0}\end{aligned}
topics.activity: Compare information bits, encoded states and the generated phase waveform.

topics.title: Minimum-shift keying
topics.definition: MSK is binary continuous-phase FSK with modulation index one half. The frequency deviation is Rb/4 from the center frequency.
topics.explanation: Each bit changes phase deviation by +π/2 or −π/2. Phase remains continuous when the sign changes; only its slope changes. The two tones are separated by Rb/2.
topics.activity: Follow the phase accumulator and see the continuous waveform through bit transitions.

topics.title: Orthogonal M-FSK
topics.definition: M-FSK selects one of M tones per symbol. The symbol represents log2M bits.
topics.explanation: The noncoherent design here uses tone spacing Rs. A larger tone set needs a wider frequency allocation. Rectangular symbol pulses also have sidelobes beyond the outer first nulls.
topics.activity: Inspect each transmitted symbol index and its tone in the serial waveform.

topics.title: Matched filtering and timed sampling
topics.definition: A matched filter maximizes output SNR at a chosen decision time for a known pulse in white Gaussian noise. Its impulse response is the reversed, delayed pulse.
topics.explanation: For a rectangular unit pulse the matched-filter output grows as the pulse enters the filter, reaches a peak at the decision time and then falls. The output is not a direct copy of the input waveform.
topics.activity: Watch the rectangular input produce the triangular matched-filter response.

topics.title: Decision regions in noise
topics.definition: A BPSK decision statistic lies near +√Eb or −√Eb, with projected noise variance N0/2. For equal priors the threshold is zero.
topics.explanation: Noise can push the received value across the threshold. The shaded tail under a conditional density is the probability of deciding the wrong symbol given that transmitted symbol. Unequal priors shift the optimum threshold.
topics.activity: Generate received statistics, compare them with the zero threshold and inspect decisions.

topics.title: BER comparison
topics.definition: BER is the probability of a bit decision error under stated assumptions. It is a statistical quantity, not the height of a time waveform.
topics.explanation: The analytical curves here compare coherent BPSK, coherent orthogonal BFSK, differential DBPSK and noncoherent orthogonal BFSK in ideal AWGN. A short simulated run fluctuates around, rather than exactly matching, the theoretical BER.
topics.activity: Change Eb/N0. Inspect the received-symbol stream and compare the analytical BER values.

topics.title: Power–bandwidth–rate trade-offs
topics.definition: A useful design reports energy, data rate, bandwidth and reliability together. Improving one quantity may cost another.
topics.explanation: Higher-order PSK or QAM can reduce symbol rate for a fixed bit rate but requires closer signal points and typically more Eb/N0 at a fixed BER. Orthogonal M-FSK has a different energy–bandwidth trade-off. Do not apply a QAM rule indiscriminately to FSK.
topics.activity: Compare spectral efficiency and the received-noise margin while changing the modulation order.
